initial_requirements: The Energy Management System is intended to monitor and manage heating and cooling activity independently of the equipment it supervises. It should evaluate temperature conditions, determine when heating or cooling resources are needed, and report important operating events. Users need a reliable way to initialize the system, review its status, and understand situations such as temperature limits or unavailable equipment.

slots.key: Inactive or reset safe state behavior
slots.value: When inactive or reset, the system should enter a safe, neutral state, make no active heating or cooling requests, keep monitoring only as needed to confirm safe resumption, report that it is not controlling the equipment, and remain inactive if sensor or equipment status is uncertain until the uncertainty clears. It should wait for valid temperature readings, confirmed equipment availability, and the normal startup check before becoming active again. If the reset happened because of a fault, it should stay inactive until the fault is cleared and acknowledged, not just until the temperature looks okay again. It should also remain inactive if the equipment keeps dropping in and out or if the readings are still unstable. If the missing or inconsistent input affects control confidence, it should fall back to a safe degraded mode and tell the operator that manual attention is needed. It should continue only if it can do so safely and should not quietly guess or keep acting as if the data were still good.

slots.key: Decision rule for delaying or allowing control actions
slots.value: Prioritize equipment and safety first, then control accuracy, and only after that responsiveness. Delay or throttle action if immediate execution could cause short cycling, violate a temperature limit, or create unstable control; allow it to proceed immediately if the risk is low and the system is within normal bounds. In startup and recovery, be more conservative and allow a short stabilization period before issuing normal control actions. During shutdown or fault handling, safety and orderly stopping override responsiveness, so immediate control can be blocked if needed. Once the system is back in normal automatic operation, the usual delay-or-proceed rule applies again. If the reading is stable and no timing constraint is active, proceed immediately; if the sensor data looks stale or uncertain, hold back until the input is trustworthy again.

slots.key: Maintenance update and change management without operational disruption
slots.value: Routine updates may include threshold adjustments, contact changes, sensor or equipment replacements, software updates, and calibration changes. These should happen without interrupting normal monitoring if possible, or with only a short, planned maintenance window. The system should keep current operating settings stable until the change is confirmed so day-to-day operations are not disrupted unexpectedly. Responsibility should usually sit with facilities or operations, since they watch building conditions day to day, while maintenance or an engineer should approve changes that affect equipment behavior or safety thresholds. The responsibility should be clear so changes are not made casually. The maintenance window should be kept as short as possible based on the risk of leaving the system partly unavailable, and simple configuration edits should keep monitoring fully live; changes touching the sensor, control interface, or core software may require a brief pause to avoid bad readings or false alerts. Changes to minimum on/off timing settings should use a controlled maintenance path rather than everyday operators, with every change recorded by who made it and when. Operators should be able to see the currently active values in the status or settings view, along with enough history to tell when a timing rule was last changed. The system should clearly indicate whether a change takes effect immediately or only after restart or reinitialization. Operators should be able to see at least the last change time, the previous value, the new value, and who made the change. A clear indicator should show whether the new value is active right now, pending restart, or only applied after reinitialization. A simple change log for the most recent few updates would make it easier to audit what timing rule is actually in force. For display preferences specifically, personal choices should take effect immediately and persist for that user after logout or restart; site-wide defaults should also persist unless an administrator changes them. Maintenance or upgrades should not reset those settings unless there is a deliberate migration or a compatibility issue that forces a reset.

slots.value: Before the system is allowed to operate, the accountable signer must confirm that sensor and equipment checks passed, the configuration is correct, and any startup exceptions are understood and accepted; acceptable exceptions include non-critical conditions where the system is not fully healthy but still safe to proceed, such as an offline sensor, a temporary equipment communication issue, a configuration warning that does not block operation, and a temperature limit condition present during startup. Before override is allowed when the system is already faulted, equipment is unavailable, or a temperature limit has been breached, the operator should acknowledge the exact fault or limit condition on screen and confirm they understand the risk. If the temperature limit has been breached, explicit approval or higher-level authorization is required rather than a routine operator click-through. Minimum on and off times should apply only when the equipment is being controlled in automatic mode, and they should not force a state change when the site is in fault, in manual override, or the equipment is unavailable. slots.key: Open issues about temperature limits or event reporting
slots.value: Temperature limits or unavailable equipment; events are understood as limit reached, equipment failure, or mode change, and the terms should be used consistently so messages and status mean the same thing every time. The records should capture temperature readings, when heating or cooling was requested, when equipment became unavailable, when limits were reached or cleared, and if replacing a previous system or manual logs, the handoff should preserve current control settings, recent temperature-related events, notable overrides or exceptions, and a reasonable window of trends or logs so operators can see what was happening before cutover. Very old routine records should stay out of the handoff, and anything containing sensitive personnel notes or irrelevant paperwork should also be excluded. A full historical archive may not be necessary.

slots.key: Retention requirements for temperature records by record type
slots.value: Routine temperature history should be kept for about 90 days; alerts and operating events for around one year; outages or limit breaches for at least three years. If a site has regulatory or contractual requirements for longer retention, the system should automatically extend the default for that site or allow a clearly documented configured override. The exact longer compliance periods still need confirmation with the customer or compliance team.

slots.value: At minimum, the readiness check should include whoever owns the building operations and whoever is responsible for the energy or facilities system. If there is a controls technician or maintenance person for the site, they should also be included. A site-specific operator can be left out if they do not manage the system day to day. If there isn’t a controls technician or maintenance person, someone from facilities or building operations should take that role, and in some sites an external service provider may fill it if they support the equipment. There does not need to be one person included by title, but there must be someone accountable for the site and someone who can confirm the system is safe to operate. The final accountable sign-off should come from the person accountable for the site’s operations, usually the facilities lead or building owner’s delegate.

slots.value: Apply the minimum on/off timing scope only in automatic control mode for now; manual override and fault handling are excluded from the same timing logic. When automatic control is paused because the equipment is unavailable, the timing rule should carry forward so the system does not immediately short-cycle when control resumes. If there is a limit breach, the system should re-evaluate from the current safe state and only resume once normal conditions and the timing rules both permit it. The delay-or-proceed rule should be more conservative during startup and recovery, with a short stabilization period before normal control actions. During shutdown or fault handling, safety and orderly stopping should override responsiveness, and immediate control can be blocked if needed. Once the system returns to normal automatic operation, the usual delay-or-proceed rule applies again.
